title: The Same Bones in Different Jobs
principle: Bones that match like this are called homologous.

t: A bat's wing, a whale's flipper and your hand. Different jobs. Same bones, in the same order.
A bat flies, a whale swims, a mole digs and you type. Open all four up and you find the same bones in the same order, just stretched differently.
sub: One long bone. Then two. Then a handful of little ones. Then fingers.
One bone, then two, then a cluster of small ones, then digits. Every time, in that order.

question: If you were building a wing from scratch, would you start with a hand?
If you were designing a wing with no constraints at all, would the arrangement of a hand be your starting point?
options: No — I would build whatever works best for flying
Yes — a hand is the obvious way to start
It would not matter either way
stages.outcome: No — I would build whatever works best for flying
note: Think about it before you look.
Commit first. Notice that an insect wing, which flies perfectly well, contains no bones at all.

t: Bones that match like this are called homologous. It means 'the same underneath'.
Structures that match part-for-part in this way are called homologous — the same underlying plan doing different jobs.

Homologous structures: the same skeletal elements in the same topological relationships, serving different functions. Contrast analogous structures, which do the same job by different means — a bird wing and an insect wing.

Homology is a claim about correspondence of parts, not of function. It is diagnosed by relative position, developmental origin and connectivity, and it is deliberately independent of what the structure is used for — otherwise it would be circular.
sub: The bat and the whale do totally different things with them.
Same parts, same order, wildly different jobs — that combination is the interesting bit.
The pattern is nested: all four limbs share the one-bone-two-bones plan, but only some share the wrist arrangement, and fewer still share particular finger reductions.
Crucially the similarities are nested rather than scattered — groups within groups — which is a far more specific pattern than mere resemblance and is what both accounts below have to explain.

t: Everyone agrees the bones match. Here is what each side says the matching means.
The anatomical correspondence is not disputed. What it licenses you to conclude is.
evidence: The bones really do correspond, part for part, across mammals, birds, reptiles and amphibians — and the correspondence is nested, with groups inside groups.
The correspondence is detailed, part-for-part, and nested: tetrapod limbs share one-bone-two-bones universally, while finer features are shared only within subgroups. Nobody disputes the anatomy.

claim: The bones match because these animals all got them from a shared ancestor.
Homology reflects common descent: the plan is shared because it was inherited, and modified afterwards for different jobs.
because: A designer starting fresh could build a wing any way at all. An inherited plan can only be bent, not replaced — which is exactly what you see.

Descent with modification predicts constrained, historically-contingent design: you can only alter what you inherited. It also explains features that are useless or actively bad — the giraffe's recurrent laryngeal nerve looping down the neck and back, the vertebrate retina wired back-to-front — which are hard to motivate as design but trivial as inherited history.
predicts: Animals that look related in their bones should also look related in their genes.
Independent character sets — bones, genes, developmental sequences, shared broken genes — should produce the same nested tree, and shared mistakes should be shared in exactly that pattern.

claim: The bones match because one Designer used one good plan many times.
Homology reflects common design: a single Designer reusing a proven engineering solution across many creatures.
because: Engineers reuse good designs all the time. Finding the same wheel on many different cars does not mean the cars had babies.

Reuse of a working module is normal engineering practice and predicts exactly this kind of shared architecture. They also argue the inference is weakened where homologous structures arise from non-homologous genes or different embryonic tissues — which, on their account, descent should not permit.
predicts: You should find the same good ideas turning up in creatures that are not related at all.

Homologous structures should sometimes be built by different genes or different developmental routes, and strikingly similar solutions should recur in distant groups — as with the eye of an octopus and the eye of a vertebrate.

ask: Both explain the matching bones. Which one also explains a mistake being copied?

Both accounts handle useful shared structure comfortably. The place they come apart is shared NON-function: broken genes, useless remnants, wiring that costs the animal something. Ask what each account predicts about those, and then ask what each would accept as a counter-example.

q: What does calling two structures homologous claim?
What is the content of a homology claim?
options: The same parts in the same order, doing different jobs
Two things that do the same job
Two things that look the same from outside
why: It is about the parts underneath, not the job on top. A bat's wing and a bee's wing both fly, but they are not homologous — there are no matching bones, because a bee has none.

Homology is correspondence of parts by position and origin, deliberately defined without reference to function. A bat wing and an insect wing are analogous — same job, no shared parts. A bat wing and a whale flipper are homologous — same parts, no shared job.

The definition is intentionally function-blind, because a function-based definition would make the concept circular. Diagnosis rests on relative position, connectivity and developmental origin, which is why an octopus eye and a vertebrate eye are analogous despite the resemblance: they develop from different tissues and are wired in opposite directions.

t: This is why medicines can be tested on mice first. The parts are close enough to tell you something.

Nearly all drug development runs through model organisms because their parts correspond to ours. Where the correspondence breaks down, so does the prediction — which is why some drugs pass in mice and fail in people.
